conclusion: Ranging over all choices of S (exhaustive over every k-subset of the first nine primes, k <= 5) does not beat the first k primes, so r_186989's flagged 'door with genuine trade shape' is slack; the sweep instead produced a proved normalization theorem (admissible sets are exactly the S-smooth dilates of primitive ones, which explains why widening the box never moved a row) and a refutation of that hunt's proposed residue lemma |A| <= p-1 for p not in S, which is false for every odd p because r+r is nonzero mod odd p. The one conjectural lemma offered is uniformly bounded height, and two natural explicit forms for its constant were killed by this run's own data.
confidence: Lean hard on the two proved items (normalization, and the repaired residue lemma with its p=3,5,7 counterexamples): they are short proofs plus witnesses re-verified by trial division, independent of any search box. Lean moderately on 'first k primes are not beaten' - it is exhaustive over the subsets and boxes stated and nothing more, and it is a claim about a maximum, which this machinery can never refute. Do not lean on the height conjecture at all: it is verified for no S, only consistent with 15 of them.

threads.what: Prime-size monotonicity is false: g({2,3,11}) = 4 (exhaustive to N=20000) while g({2,3,13}) >= 5. 29 such violations in the sweep.
threads.why_it_might_matter: Any S-level lemma must be stated in terms of a prime's additive position relative to the S-smooth semigroup, not its size. It also blocks the obvious route to proving first-k-primes optimality.

threads.what: Height is not monotone in k: h({2,3,7,13}) = 159 at k=4 but h({2,3,5,7,11,13}) = 47 at k=6.
threads.why_it_might_matter: It rules out the naive induction on k for the bounded-height conjecture, and says a proof will have to be about S rather than about |S|.
threads.first_step: Compute h for a few hundred random S of size 4-6 drawn from the first 25 primes and look at the distribution rather than the max.

threads.what: The second gap for finitising g(k): bounding which primes may appear in a maximizing S.
threads.why_it_might_matter: Bounded height alone finitises g(S) for fixed S, not g(k). Nothing here bounds the primes, and the monotonicity failure says it is not trivial.

core_candidates.what: A smooth-sum clique solver that builds edges from the smooth sums (s smooth, s = a+b) instead of scanning O(N^2) pairs.
core_candidates.why_reusable: It is what made an exhaustive sweep over 381 choices of S affordable inside one support run; the r_186989 version needed minutes per row where this needs sub-second. Any additive-smoothness search (Erdos-Turan style problems, S-unit equations, Sidon-with-constraints) has the same shape: few admissible sums, many candidate elements.
